title: Polite requests and opinions
cando: ask politely, agree and disagree, and give an opinion with a reason

about.text: In this lesson you give your opinion, and you agree and disagree politely. You ask for things at a desk with could and would. Then you write a polite note.
goals: Give an opinion: I think …, I'm sure …, I doubt …
Agree and disagree politely, with a reason: I agree, because …
Ask politely: Could you …? Would you mind …?
Say what is not allowed and what is not necessary: mustn't, don't need to.
Make a request at a desk, and give your opinion in a meeting.

chapters.title: Two views on a bus route
chapters.text:
In this lesson you give your opinion, and you ask for things politely.
First, you listen to two colleagues, Ana and Samir. The number 12 bus is going to change its route.
Samir says: I think it's a good idea. Ana says: Sorry, I disagree.
Later, Ana says: I agree, because I'm often late too.
They both give a reason. That is the important part.
Listen to their voices. When you are sure, your voice goes down at the end.

chapters.title: I think, could and mustn't
chapters.text:
After I think, I hope and I'm sure, say a whole sentence. I think the bus is too slow. I hope they listen to us.
For no, say: I don't think it's fair.
To ask politely, use could or would. Could you help me? Would you mind waiting?
Could is more polite than can.
Mustn't and don't need to are different.
You mustn't park here. It is not allowed.
You don't need to pay. It is free, so it is not necessary.

chapters.title: Asking at a desk
chapters.text:
Next, you read a short text: How to ask for something at a desk.
It gives four steps. Start with Excuse me. Use could or would. Say thank you. And be patient.
It also explains a difficult answer. Do you mind waiting? No, not at all. That means: yes, I can wait.
Then you write a polite note. You ask for two things.

chapters.title: At the desk, then in the meeting
chapters.text:
In the task, you visit another office. At reception, you ask for a visitor's pass and the Wi-Fi password.
Use could, or would you mind, and say thank you.
Then you are in a short meeting. Your manager asks: Should we start work at eight?
Give your opinion and a reason. Then agree or disagree with a colleague.
Say: I see your point, but I think …

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a story about asking and opinions.
Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.

warmup.prompt: Your bus company wants to change your bus route. What do you do?
choices: I tell the company my opinion.
I talk to my friends about it.
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Many people say nothing. But companies often ask for opinions, and a short, polite message can help.

conversation.title: Two views on a bus route
conversation.setting: Ana and Samir work at the same hotel. At lunch, they read a notice about the number 12 bus.
lines: Samir
Have you seen this notice? The number 12 bus is going to change its route.
Ana
Yes, I read it this morning. What's your opinion?
Samir
I think it's a good idea. The new route is much faster.
Ana
Sorry, I disagree. It won't stop at the hospital any more.
Samir
Hmm, that's a good point. But I believe more people will use it.
Ana
I doubt it. A lot of older people need that stop. It's unfair.
Samir
I understand your view. But the old route is so slow. People complain every day.
Ana
I agree, because I'm often late for work too!
Samir
I suppose they could keep one stop at the hospital.
Ana
Yes! Imagine a fast bus that still stops at the hospital.
Samir
I'm sure people will approve of that. It's fair to everybody.
Ana
Let's write to the bus company. I hope they listen to us.
Samir
They promised to answer everybody. Could you write the email? You're better at it.
Ana
OK. I'm not sure they'll change anything, but good public transport is important.

questions.q: Why does Samir like the new route?
questions.why: Samir says: The new route is much faster.

questions.q: Why does Ana disagree at first?
questions.a: The bus won't stop at the hospital.
wrong: The new route is too slow.
questions.why: Ana says: It won't stop at the hospital any more.

questions.a: write an email to the bus company
questions.why: Samir asks: Could you write the email? Ana says: OK.

phrases.text: I think it's a good idea.

phrases.use: Saying politely that you think something different.
Saying the other person is right about one thing.
Saying you don't know, or you only half agree.

items.meaning: What you think about something.
items.example: In my opinion, the new timetable is better.

items.meaning: To think that something is true.
items.example: I believe the office opens at nine, but please check.

items.meaning: To have a different opinion from another person.
items.example: I'm sorry, but I disagree with you.

items.meaning: To think something is probably true, but you are not sure.
items.example: It's after ten. I suppose the shops are closed now.

items.meaning: To think that something is probably not true.
items.example: I doubt the train will be on time. It's snowing.

items.meaning: To make a picture of something in your mind.
items.example: Imagine a city with no cars!

items.meaning: To think something is good or right. We often say approve of.
items.example: Most residents approve of the new park.

items.meaning: One idea or fact in a discussion.
items.example: That's a good point. I didn't think of that.

items.meaning: What you think about something. It means the same as opinion.
items.example: In my view, the rent is too high.

items.meaning: Buses, trains and trams that everybody can use.
items.example: I don't drive. I use public transport.

items.meaning: Right and good, and the same for everybody.
items.example: Everybody works one Saturday a month. That's fair.

items.meaning: Not right, because it is not the same for everybody.
items.example: It's unfair. I always work late, and he never does.

items.meaning: To say that something is wrong and you are not happy about it.
items.example: We complained to the landlord about the noise.

items.meaning: To say that you will really do something.
items.example: I promise I'll call you tomorrow.

sound.title: Down when you are sure, up when you ask
sound.explain: Your voice tells people what you mean. When you are sure, your voice goes down at the end. When you ask a yes or no question, it often goes up. Listen, then say each pair.
groups: The bus is late. · The bus is late?
lines: I think it's a good idea.
Sorry, I disagree.
Could you write the email?

sayIt.instructions: Say Ana's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Does your voice go down when you are sure?
lines: Yes, I read it this morning. What's your opinion?
Sorry, I disagree. It won't stop at the hospital any more.
I agree, because I'm often late for work too!
Let's write to the bus company. I hope they listen to us.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. Four give an opinion or a hope. The last one asks for something.
examples: I think it's a good idea.
I believe more people will use it.
I hope they listen to us.
I'm sure people will approve of that.
spot.question: What comes after I think, I believe, I hope and I'm sure? How does Samir ask Ana to write the email?
spot.answer: After I think, I believe, I hope and I'm sure comes a whole sentence. It has its own person and verb: it's a good idea. Samir uses could: Could you write the email? Could makes the request polite.

rules.title: I think, I hope, I'm sure + a sentence
rule: I think, I hope, I'm sure + a whole sentence: I think the bus is slow.
I believe (that) it will help. You can add that, or leave it out.
Not sure? I suppose it's OK. I doubt it will change. I'm not sure.
For no, put not with think: I don't think it's fair.
Agree or disagree with a reason: I agree, because … / I see your point, but …
rules.mistake: Not: I am agree with you. Say: I agree with you.

rules.title: Could you …? Would you mind …? · mustn't or don't need to
rule: Could you + a verb: Could you help me, please? Could I have a copy?
Would you mind + -ing: Would you mind waiting? — No, not at all.
Could is more polite than can. Use it with people you don't know.
mustn't = it is not allowed: You mustn't park here.
don't need to = it is not necessary: You don't need to book. Just come.
rules.mistake: Not: You mustn't pay. It's free. Say: You don't need to pay. It's free.

practice.why: For no, say I don't think + a sentence.

practice.q: I'm ___ the office opens at nine. I checked on the website.
practice.why: I'm sure + a sentence. You checked, so you are sure.

practice.q: I ___ with you. The new route is better.
practice.why: Say I agree, not I am agree.
Could you + a verb makes a polite request.

practice.q: Would you mind if I sit here? — No, ___ .
practice.why: No, not at all means: it's no problem.

practice.q: You ___ park here. It's for ambulances only.
practice.why: It is not allowed, so use mustn't.

practice.q: You ___ pay for the course. It's free.
practice.why: It is free, so paying is not necessary: don't need to.

practice.q: ___ I have a copy of the form, please?
practice.why: Could I …? asks for something politely.

practice.q: It's after ten. I ___ the shop is closed now.
practice.why: I suppose: I think it's probably true, but I'm not sure.

yourTurn.prompt: Your town wants to change the car park in the centre into a small park. What do you think? Write three or four sentences. Give your opinion and a reason.
starters: I agree, because … / I disagree, because …
yourTurn.model: I think it's a good idea. The town centre is too noisy and crowded. I'm sure people will enjoy a park. But I don't think it's fair to drivers, because the buses are slow.

text.title: How to ask for something at a desk
text.body:
Every day, we ask people for things. It can be a form, a key or a minute of their time. Here are four steps for a polite request.

1. Start with Excuse me, or Sorry to bother you. The person at reception is often busy.
2. Use could or would. Could I have a visitor's pass, please? Would you mind checking my booking?
3. Say thank you, even for a small thing. People really appreciate it.
4. Be patient. When there is a long queue, patience helps everybody.

Do you need something bigger? Ask: Could you do me a favour? Then say what it is.

Somebody asks: Do you mind waiting? If you can wait, say: No, not at all.

You don't need to speak perfect English. But you mustn't forget please and thank you. Give me a form! is rude, even with please at the end.

Are you late? One short excuse is enough. Say sorry once, and then say what you need.

gist.a: how to ask for things politely
wrong: how to get a job at reception
gist.why: It gives four steps for a polite request.

detail.q: The person at reception is busy. What can you say first?
detail.why: Step 1 says: Start with Excuse me, or Sorry to bother you.

detail.q: Somebody asks: Do you mind waiting? You can wait. What do you say?
detail.why: No, not at all means: it's no problem, I can wait.

detail.q: Why is Give me a form! a problem?
detail.a: It is rude, even with please.
detail.why: The text says: Give me a form! is rude, even with please at the end.

detail.q: You are late. What does the text say?
detail.a: Give one short excuse, and say sorry once.
detail.why: One short excuse is enough. Say sorry once.

items.meaning: When you ask for something in a polite way.
items.example: The hotel said yes to my request for a quiet room.

items.meaning: Something kind that you do for somebody because they ask.
items.example: Could you do me a favour and water my plants?

items.meaning: To feel that something is a problem for you. Do you mind …? asks politely.
items.example: Do you mind if I open the window?

items.meaning: Kind and careful in the way you speak to people.
items.example: The receptionist was very polite and helpful.

items.meaning: Not polite.
items.example: The man in the queue was very rude to the staff.

items.meaning: A reason you give when you did something wrong, like being late.
items.example: He always has an excuse for being late.

items.meaning: To stop somebody when they are busy, to ask them something.
items.example: Sorry to bother you. Can I ask a quick question?

items.meaning: The desk near the door of a hotel, a clinic or an office. People there help visitors.
items.example: Please ask at reception for your key.

items.meaning: Waiting calmly, without getting angry.
items.example: Thank you for your patience. The doctor will see you soon.

items.meaning: To be grateful for something.
items.example: I really appreciate your help.

model.title: A polite note
model.body:
Dear Lena,
Sorry to bother you. I have two small requests.
Could I have a new key card, please? Mine doesn't open the door any more.
And would you mind booking the meeting room for me on Friday at ten?
I really appreciate your help.
Thank you,
Carlos (Room 14)

write.task: Write a polite note to a receptionist or a colleague. It can be real or made up. Ask for two things. Use could once and would you mind once. Say thank you at the end.
write.starter: Dear …, Sorry to bother you. Could I …
checklist: I used could once and would you mind once.
I said please and thank you.
I didn't use Give me or I want.

card.title: At the desk, then in the meeting
card.situation: You are visiting your company's other office for a meeting. At reception, you need a visitor's pass and the Wi-Fi password. In the meeting, your manager asks: Should we start work at eight instead of nine?
card.goal: Make two polite requests at reception. Then give your opinion in the meeting, with a reason. Agree or disagree politely with one colleague.

phrases: Excuse me. Could I have a visitor's pass, please?
Would you mind telling me the Wi-Fi password?
Thank you. I really appreciate it.
I think it's a good idea, because …
I see your point, but I don't think …
prepare.notes: Make notes. What two things do you need at reception? What do you think about starting at eight? Write one reason.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher is the receptionist. Make your two requests. Then the class has a short meeting. Everybody gives an opinion with a reason, and agrees or disagrees with one person.
doIt.wehel: First, you are a receptionist at an office. I will ask you for two things. Then you are my manager in a meeting. Ask me: Should we start work at eight instead of nine? Disagree with me once, politely. Use simple English.

model.title: At reception, and in the meeting
lines: Receptionist
Good morning. Can I help you?
You
Good morning. Could I have a visitor's pass, please? I'm here for the ten o'clock meeting.
Receptionist
Of course. What's your name, please?
You
Omar Haddad. And would you mind telling me the Wi-Fi password?
Receptionist
Not at all. It's on this card.
You
Thank you. I really appreciate it.
Manager
So, should we start work at eight instead of nine? What do you think, Omar?
You
I think it's a good idea, because the roads are quieter at eight.
Priya
I disagree. The buses are very crowded at half past seven.
You
That's a good point, Priya. I suppose some people could start at nine.
Manager
So maybe people can choose: eight or nine?
You
I agree, because that's fair to everybody.
Manager
Good. I promise I'll talk to the director this week.
compare: Did you use could or would you mind at reception?
Did you give your opinion with a reason: I think …, because …?
Did you agree or disagree politely: That's a good point. I see your point, but …?

canDo: I can give my opinion with I think, I'm sure and I doubt.
I can agree and disagree politely, and give a reason.
I can ask for things politely with could and would you mind.
I can use mustn't and don't need to for rules.
I can write a polite note with two requests.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first picture. Where are the people? What do you think they disagree about?
reading.talk: Who was right in the story, in your opinion? Why? Write two or three sentences with I think … because …, or say them to Wehel.

quiz.why: After I don't think comes a whole sentence: it's fair.

quiz.q: Could you ___ me the way to reception, please?
quiz.why: Could you + a verb: Could you tell me …?

quiz.q: You ___ smoke in the building. It's not allowed.
quiz.why: It is not allowed, so use mustn't.

quiz.q: That's a good ___ . I didn't think of that.
quiz.why: A point is one idea in a discussion.

quiz.q: Somebody asks: Do you mind waiting? You're happy to wait. What do you say?
quiz.why: No, not at all means: it's no problem.
Public transport is buses, trains and trams that everybody can use.

quiz.q: There are ___ people in the shop today than yesterday.
quiz.why: You can count people, so use fewer.

quiz.q: How long ___ you lived in this flat?
quiz.why: How long + have you + the past form: How long have you lived …?

quiz.q: The film was so ___ that I fell asleep.
quiz.why: -ing tells you about the thing: the film was boring.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the bus route conversation in pairs. Then change the topic: a new car park, longer shop hours, a new timetable. Each learner gives one opinion with because.
Day 2: a polite request round. Each learner asks for something with Could you …? or Would you mind …?, and the others answer. Then read two rules aloud and say mustn't or don't need to.
Day 3: the task. You are the receptionist, then the manager. Each learner makes two requests, then gives an opinion in a short meeting and agrees or disagrees politely.
Day 4: talk about the book, answer questions, and read two learners' polite notes aloud.
